newsitem.title: UK: British shares slide, weak Wall St spooks market.
newsitem.headline: British shares slide, weak Wall St spooks market.

text.p: Around 11 billion pounds ($18 billion) was wiped off the value of British shares on Friday as investors ran for cover after another sharp sell-off of U.S. shares on Wall Street.

The chant of "the market giveth, the market taketh away" may have been heard in British share dealing rooms on Friday as Thursday's 52-point surge to a record high was completely erased after a near 70-point plunge in the U.S. share market.

The Financial Times Index of top 100 leading British shares closed 52.7 points lower at 4,218.8, mirroring a similar slide by the Dow Industrials Average of the 30 leading U.S. shares, which was off 68 points by the London close.
A profits warning from one of Britain's leading supermarket chains also undermined market confidence but share strategists believe the FTSE is only pausing for breath before testing new highs.
"Fundamentally, we are still bullish of the British share market," said Corey Miller, shares strategist at French investment bank Credit Lyonnais Laing.
"Markets on both sides of the Atlantic have performed strongly so it's to be expected that we now have a bit of profit-taking."

Miller, like many share strategists predicts that low interest rates and subdued inflation will continue to enourage investors to buy shares, since the alternative is to put their cash into bank and building society accounts which only low rates of return.
Only 24 hours earlier, the FTSE had finished at a record high of 4,271.5, prompting some market watchers to predict the top 100 index could hit its year-end target levels by the end of the month.

But the Dow's near 94-point slide on Thursday and the weaker start on Friday raised fears that the U.S. share market may be about to fall even more sharply in the coming weeks -- a move that would take British shares lower in its wake.

"The market feels there is going to be a U.S. correction but it may not start just yet," the head of trading at a large stockbroker said. "I suspect both the U.S. and British markets will have a breather but volatility will rule."
The share trader noted that over the past few months, the Dow has regularly fallen 50 to 100 points in a day, only to recover the lost ground and reach record highs.
"Wall Street's raging bull is a hard animal to stop. It may run out of steam temporarily but with so many strategists still expecting more gains it is dangerous to stand in its way."

Up to yesterday's close the Dow had gone up 307.48 points or 4.77 percent since the beginning of the year. The FTSE 100 meanwhile had gained 153 points or 3.7 percent but gave back over one percent of that advance today.
Among individual shares, Britain leading supermarket chain J. Sainsbury Plc led food retailers lower after the company warned that full-year profits would be below market expectations.
Sainsbury shares plunged 52-1/2p or 13 percent to 339-1/2p, Safeway fell 13-1/2p to 389p, Tesco slipped 9p to 359p, Kwiksave lost 11-1/2p to 307p and Asda eased 2-1/4p to 122p.
